description: Learn about ionization methods, mass analyzers, tandem MS, and quantitative proteomics.

slides.title: Welcome to Mass Spectrometry
slides.content:
# Mass Spectrometry

Welcome to **Mass Spectrometry (MS)**!

## What You Will Learn:
- **Ionization methods** - Making proteins fly
- **Mass analyzers** - Sorting by weight
- **Tandem MS** - Breaking proteins apart to read them
- **Quantitative proteomics** - Counting the proteins

Mass Spectrometry is the core technology driving the entire field of Proteomics.

slides.title: The Principle of MS
slides.content:
# The Core Principle

Mass spectrometry measures exactly one thing: the **Mass-to-Charge ratio (m/z)** of an ion.

## The Three Steps:
1. **Ionization:** You must turn your biological sample into a gas of charged ions.
2. **Analysis:** You sort the ions based on their weight (mass) and charge using electric or magnetic fields.
3. **Detection:** You count how many ions hit the detector at each specific m/z value.

slides.title: The Problem with Proteins
slides.content:
# The Ionization Problem

For decades, physicists used MS to analyze small, sturdy molecules.

But proteins are massive, fragile, and covered in water. If you try to vaporize a protein by heating it, it simply burns and turns to charcoal.

To analyze proteins, scientists had to invent **Soft Ionization** techniques that could lift a heavy protein into the gas phase without shattering it.

slides.title: MALDI
slides.content:
# MALDI Ionization

**Matrix-Assisted Laser Desorption/Ionization (MALDI)**

## How it works:
1. The protein sample is mixed with a chemical "matrix" and dried on a metal plate, forming crystals.
2. A powerful laser blasts the crystal.
3. The matrix absorbs the laser energy (protecting the fragile protein) and vaporizes, carrying the intact protein into the gas phase and giving it a charge.

slides.title: Electrospray Ionization (ESI)
slides.content:
# Electrospray Ionization (ESI)

ESI is the other major soft ionization technique.

## How it works:
The liquid protein sample is pumped through a tiny, highly electrically charged metal needle.

As the liquid exits the needle, it turns into a fine mist of charged droplets. As the liquid evaporates, the electrical charge concentrates until the droplet explodes, leaving only naked, charged proteins floating in a vacuum!

slides.title: Ionization Quiz
slides.content: Test your knowledge of making proteins fly.
slides.quizQuestion: Why do we use 'Soft Ionization' techniques like MALDI and ESI for proteomics?
quizOptions: Because hard ionization requires too much electricity
Because proteins are fragile and would burn or shatter if vaporized using traditional heat
Because proteins are already naturally in a gaseous state
To prevent the machine from getting dirty

slides.title: Mass Analyzers
slides.content:
# Mass Analyzers

Once you have a cloud of flying protein ions, you need to sort them.

## The Time of Flight (TOF) Analyzer:
This is the simplest analyzer. You place the ions at the start of a long vacuum tube and give them all the exact same electrical push.

Basic physics says: light things accelerate faster than heavy things. You simply measure the exact time it takes for them to fly down the tube and hit the detector!

slides.title: Quadrupoles and Orbitraps
slides.content:
# Advanced Analyzers

## The Quadrupole:
Uses four parallel metal rods with oscillating electrical currents. It acts as a filter, allowing only ions of one specific mass to pass through at a time, while all others crash into the rods.

## The Orbitrap:
The most advanced modern analyzer. Ions are injected into a spindle-shaped electrode and orbit around it. By measuring the complex radio frequencies of their orbits, computers can determine their mass with mind-blowing precision.

slides.title: Tandem MS (MS/MS)
slides.content:
# Tandem Mass Spectrometry

Knowing the exact mass of a protein isn't enough to know its amino acid sequence.

To "read" the sequence, we use **Tandem MS (MS/MS)**, which links two mass analyzers together with a collision chamber in the middle.

slides.title: Collision-Induced Dissociation
slides.content:
# How MS/MS Works

## Step 1: Isolation
The first mass analyzer isolates a single, specific peptide (a chopped-up piece of protein) and throws away everything else.

## Step 2: Fragmentation (CID)
The isolated peptide is fired into a chamber filled with inert Argon gas. The high-speed collisions literally break the peptide apart, specifically snapping the bonds between the amino acids.

## Step 3: Analysis
The second mass analyzer measures the mass of all the broken pieces.

slides.title: Peptide Sequencing
slides.content:
# Reading the Sequence

Because the peptide breaks randomly, you get pieces of every possible length.

By comparing the masses of a piece with 5 amino acids to a piece with 6 amino acids, the difference in mass tells you exactly which specific amino acid was in the 6th position!

Computers can do this math in milliseconds, sequencing thousands of proteins from a single cell in a single run.

slides.title: Tandem MS Quiz
slides.content: Verify your understanding of protein sequencing.
slides.quizQuestion: What is the purpose of the collision chamber in Tandem MS (MS/MS)?
quizOptions: To gently slow the proteins down before detection
To clean the proteins of any remaining water
To intentionally smash the peptide into fragments so the amino acid sequence can be read

slides.title: Quantitative Proteomics
slides.content:
# Quantitative Proteomics

Identifying which proteins are present is good, but knowing exactly *how many* of them are present is better.

If you want to compare a healthy cell to a cancer cell, you need to know which proteins the cancer cell is overproducing.

However, standard Mass Spectrometry is not inherently quantitative. We have to use clever chemical tricks.

slides.title: SILAC
slides.content:
# SILAC Labeling

**Stable Isotope Labeling by/in Amino acids in Cell culture (SILAC)**

## The Heavy Isotope Trick:
You grow the healthy cells in normal media. You grow the cancer cells in media where the amino acids are made with "Heavy" isotopes (like Carbon-13 instead of Carbon-12).

You mix the cells together and run the MS. Because the cancer proteins are slightly heavier, they show up as distinct twin peaks on the graph. The ratio of the peak heights tells you exactly how much the protein levels changed!

slides.title: iTRAQ
slides.content:
# iTRAQ Labeling

SILAC is great for cells in a petri dish, but you can't feed "heavy" carbon to a human patient to test their tissue.

## Chemical Tags:
**iTRAQ** (Isobaric Tags for Relative and Absolute Quantitation) solves this. After you extract the proteins from the human tissue, you chemically glue a chemical tag to them.

The tags act like barcodes. When the peptide is smashed in the MS/MS chamber, the tag breaks off and creates a specific reporter peak on the graph, allowing you to quantify multiple patient samples at once.

slides.title: Summary of Mass Spectrometry
slides.content:
# MS Summary

## Key Takeaways:
- **MALDI** and **ESI** are soft ionization methods that vaporize fragile proteins without breaking them.
- **TOF**, **Quadrupoles**, and **Orbitraps** sort the ions based on their mass-to-charge (m/z) ratio.
- **Tandem MS (MS/MS)** smashes peptides with gas to determine their exact amino acid sequence.
- **SILAC** and **iTRAQ** use heavy isotopes or chemical tags to turn MS into a strictly quantitative tool for comparing healthy vs diseased states.

slides.title: Module Complete
slides.content:
# Congratulations!

You have completed the Mass Spectrometry module.

You now understand the primary tool used to explore the proteome.
